chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Sukayn, from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
"There is no prayer after 'Asr until Maghrib, and no prayer after Fajr until the sun rises."

These narrations and those similar to them are interpreted as referring to the initiation of voluntary prayers during these times, rather than making up missed prayers; and the first narrations are interpreted as referring to making up missed prayers, rather than initiation, and there is no contradiction between them.

And that which indicates the distinction we mentioned is what was narrated: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Bilal, who said: I wrote to him regarding making up the voluntary prayer from the rising of dawn until the rising of the sun, and from after 'Asr until the sun sets, so he wrote: "That is not permissible except for the one who missed it; as for others, it is not permissible."
And it has been narrated that there is a concession regarding prayer at the time of the sun's rising and at the time of its setting.

-(697) 155 - Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali narrated, saying: A group of our scholars narrated to me from Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Asadi (may Allah be pleased with him): That which came to him among the answers to his questions from Muhammad ibn 'Uthman al-'Amri (may Allah sanctify his soul) was: "As for what you asked about regarding prayer at the time of the sun's rising and at the time of its setting, if the people say that the sun rises between the horns of the devil and sets between the horns of the devil, then what is better for humbling the devil than prayer? So pray it and humble the devil."
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And whoever wishes to stand in the last part of the night, to his saying: 'And whoever stands in the last part of his night.'

key_terms.بَيْنَ قَرْنَيْ شَيْطَانٍ: Between the horns of the devil (idiom for sun's rising/setting)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between making up voluntary prayers and initiating new ones during prohibited times in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between prohibitive and permissive narrations by distinguishing between initiating new voluntary prayers (makruh) and making up missed ones (ja'iz), a nuance confirmed by the Imam’s specific reply to Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar. The text further highlights the spiritual strategy of 'humbling the devil' (ar-gham anfu al-shaytan) by praying during the exact moments of his exaltation at sunrise and sunset, reflecting the Shia emphasis on ritual precision and metaphysical symbolism.
